extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of science, scientists and logicians interested in the logic of induction
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and cautions for forming, judging, and applying inductive generalizations (both universal and approximate), especially distinctions between co-existence vs succession, the role of causation, limits of empirical laws, and how to treat ‘most A are B’ claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inapplicability of elimination to co-existences
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is no general axiom standing in the same relation to the uniformities of co-existence as the law of causation does to those of succession.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Methods of Agreement or Difference, or of Concomitant Variations, which rely on elimination, are inapplicable to questions of co-existence (e.g., whether all crows are black) because there is no analogue of ‘every event has a cause’ for co-existent properties. Do not attempt to use elimination to deduce an invariable co-existent for a property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ultimate properties from causation-dependent properties
rubrics_metrics.description: If blackness (or another property) is an ultimate property of a Kind it is qualitatively different from a property that is the effect of causes; if it depends on causes it is an empirical law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a property is intrinsic to a Kind or produced by extrinsic causes. If causal, treat the generalization empirically (search for causes and common causal circumstances). If purportedly ultimate, be aware it can only be refuted by discovery of a new Kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure certainty by improbability of unnoticed exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of certainty of any generalization which rests on no other evidence than the agreement of all past observation is the degree of improbability that an exception, if any existed, could have hitherto remained unobserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the question as: how improbable is it that an exception has so far escaped observation? Consider both possibilities for an alleged exception (accident/causal variation vs new Kind) and assess which is more plausible given observational limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical-law status for causation-dependent uniformities
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities that are results of causation, or that appear to be, must be accepted only as empirical laws limited to the space of observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When properties are effects of causes, many affirmative instances with no negatives support a common cause and justify treating the generalization as universal within observed limits and with allowable extension to adjacent cases. Remain cautious about global universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability of Kind-based generalizations to discovery of new Kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: If a property is a property of Kind, the generalization can only be set aside by the discovery of a new Kind of thing not hitherto distinguished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that discovery of overlooked species, races, or subclasses (even in well-explored regions) is common; thus even Kind-based generalizations remain empirical and should be open to revision on credible witness or specimen evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require examination of all sub-kinds for high-level generalizations (unless causal link exists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Such generalizations ... ought to be grounded on an examination of all the infimæ species comprehended in them, and not of a portion only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer that a property true of several species will hold for all species in a superior Kind without either (a) a proved or presumed causal connection, or (b) explicit examination of each sub-kind. Use interpolative caution where species vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalities gain reliability with greater generality (but remain empirical)
rubrics_metrics.description: As empirical laws approach a point of high generality they become more certain; the more general they are, the more they may be depended on—yet they are still empirical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More general empirical laws suggest robustness (fewer counteracting causes across many cases) and thus require stronger evidence to overturn, but they are not exempt from being empirical and revisable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify and use approximate generalizations (Most A are B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximate generalizations are propositions of the form 'Most A are B' and their degree of probability depends on the proportion of instances that accord with the generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as valuable for practice and as steps toward universal truths, but recognize their limited deductive power (combining with other approximates often yields inconclusive results) and the need to know the underlying causes where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish two cases for admissibility of 'Most A are B'
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'Most A are B' composes the whole of our knowledge vs when it is only the most available form of more detailed knowledge (we know causes or distinguishing marks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only the approximate generalization is known, accept it only as empirical within observed limits. If causes or marks are known, use them (indirect mode) to test or apply the proposition more reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double modes for ascertaining an approximate generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: We have a direct mode (observing frequency of B among A) and an indirect mode (examining whether the causes or marks of B are frequent among A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use whichever mode is more available: observe many instances, or assess frequency of the cause/mark. Often both are combined; each can corroborate the other (example: literacy inferred from school attendance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer certain marks over approximate generalizations in individual cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever we can actually recognize the existence of the cause or mark in the individual case, we should replace the uncertain indication by a certain one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating a particular instance (e.g., whether to believe a witness), if you can check individual marks (honesty, interest, accuracy) do so rather than relying solely on the background approximate generalization that 'most persons speak truth'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply averages only to average cases; adjust when specific information exists
rubrics_metrics.description: A general average should only be applied to cases which are neither known, nor can be presumed, to be other than average cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you know species, variety, or particular circumstances of an instance, do not apply a genus-level average—use species-specific data or account for the particular circumstances. Averages are most useful for large-number problems (insurance tables), less so for single cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical precision and limits when using approximate generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: If it can be established that nine out of every ten A are B, there will be one chance in ten of error in assuming any A is a B—but only within the time, place, and circumstance of the observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When numerical frequencies are available, translate them into corresponding probabilities for individual-instance inference, but always constrain the inference to the observational domain and avoid transfer to unobserved sub-classes or circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining approximate generalizations: addition vs deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: When combining two approximate generalizations they may cooperate either by Addition (each separately applicable; combined probability greater) or by Ratiocination/Deduction (one applies only via the other; combined probability less).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether premises are independently applicable (e.g., two independent witnesses—addition) or dependent (e.g., one witness heard the other—deduction). The mode affects whether combined evidence strengthens or weakens probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against Bacon's universal application of elimination to properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon's error was to apply the principle of elimination, used for successions, to co-existences; he treated properties as if each had an invariable co-existent 'form'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid seeking a single invariant concomitant ('form') for properties like hardness, hotness, etc.; such attempts usually fail because objects that share one property rarely share a uniform set of other circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presume properties of organized beings are derivative and causation-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Organized beings, being eminently modifiable and having had a beginning, give reason to believe that none of their properties are ultimate but all are derivative, and produced by causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat biological/organismic generalizations as likely depending on complex causal networks; expect high individual and temporal variability and seek causal explanations rather than assuming ultimate, invariant properties.
